title: Sophisticated tasks need only extremely simple underlying rules

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Sophisticated tasks need only extremely simple underlying rules

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: Contrary to engineering experience, performing sophisticated tasks does not require correspondingly complicated basic rules; extremely simple underlying rules, potentially implementable directly at the atomic scale, are often sufficient.

fields.label: Chapter
fields.value: Ch. 1: The Foundations for a New Kind of Science

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: extremely simple underlying rules—that might for example potentially be implemented directly at the level of atoms—are often all that is needed.

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci A New Kind of Science claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: Stephen Wolfram, A New Kind of Science (Champaign, IL: Wolfram Media, 2002), Chapter 1, “The Foundations for a New Kind of Science”; section “Relations to Other Areas” (from p. 7), p. 11. Scope: technology and engineered systems, including nanotechnology

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on wolfram2002-ch01-12: partially-resolvable, resolvability 0.41

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Individual existence claims can be tested computationally with current resources. The frequency claim and proposed atomic implementation span a much broader design space than existing catalogs support.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Define task sophistication, rule description length, and required reliability, then search public program spaces for compact rules that meet task benchmarks. One verified compact implementation establishes sufficiency for that task, but frequencies are needed to test often.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Sophisticated and extremely simple depend on encoding.

Atomic-scale implementability is separate from computational sufficiency.

Existing catalogs cover few engineered tasks.

fields.value:

data existence: 0.45
analysis feasibility: 0.35
discriminating power: 0.5
operationalizability: 0.45

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Published universality shows that some sophisticated computations have very small rule tables, so the existential reading is checkable now. The claim that extremely simple rules are often all that engineering needs, and that they are implementable directly at atomic scale, ranges over technology that has not been catalogued in that form. Existing proofs therefore settle a weakened reading and leave the practical frequency open.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Take a list of sophisticated computational tasks and ask whether each has an implementation whose rule text is short, with task complexity counted separately from the initial condition. The weak reading is confirmed by one universal one-sentence rule. The engineering reading, including atomic-scale implementation, needs a demonstrated device whose physical rule, not only its abstract encoding, is extremely simple.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
A universal rule shifts the task's complexity into the initial condition.

Atomic-scale implementation is an engineering prediction without a systematic public inventory of such devices.
